query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a refractory alumina (Al2O3) coating on components (such as rollers and guide plates) in hot dip aluminum plating equipment will reduce the erosion by molten aluminum and thereby extend the service life of these parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional metal components (typically steel) that are vulnerable to aluminum-induced corrosion and erosion in the hot dip process.
generation.intervention: Applying a dense, well-bonded, high-purity alumina (Al2O3) coating or using pre-formed alumina refractory parts in critical areas of the equipment.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum during the hot dip plating process with typical thermal cycling and mechanical stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and maintenance of a stable, self-healing, inert alumina layer at the surface that acts as a diffusion barrier between the liquid aluminum and the underlying metal substrate.
generation.mechanism: The alumina layer substantially reduces chemical reactivity with liquid aluminum because it is chemically inert and has a high melting point, thus diminishing dissolution and erosion of the substrate. The coating’s self-healing nature under high-temperature conditions may also mitigate minor coating defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated components will exhibit a significantly lower rate of erosion and corrosion in contact with molten aluminum, resulting in a longer service life when compared to unprotected metal parts.
generation.baseline: Uncoated, conventional metal parts that suffer rapid material loss and degradation due to prolonged exposure to corrosive, high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: The protective performance may be compromised by factors such as coating defects, insufficient adhesion, thermal fatigue, or spallation under repetitive thermal-mechanical cycling. In addition, the coating process must be compatible with the geometry and operational demands of the plating equipment.
generation.uncertainty: While alumina is known for its inertness and stability at high temperatures, the long-term durability of an alumina coating under the specific cyclic conditions of hot dip aluminum plating (including potential mechanical stresses and thermal shock) requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical dipping/plating equipment components—one group with an applied dense alumina coating and one group left uncoated. Operate both sets under real-world hot dip aluminum plating conditions for an extended period. Regularly inspect and measure surface degradation, mass loss, and microstructure changes.
measurements: Weight loss per unit area over time
Surface morphology and coating integrity via microscopy
Changes in mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, integrity) after cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the coated components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion/erosion rates compared to the uncoated components or if the alumina coating degrades (e.g., spalls or cracks) such that it fails to provide effective protection under the test conditions.
